idiom_name: initialise() called from main + RAII members
implementation_notes: The modern default: one initialise() runs from main() (or from the owning component's constructor) and returns an error instead of relying on pre-main magic, while the acquired resources are RAII members, so release happens deterministically on every exit path including exceptions. Reach for std::call_once or a function-local static only when the acquisition can also be entered concurrently from a second entry point: both are specified to initialise exactly once under concurrency, and function-local statics are noted as possibly more efficient than the equivalent std::call_once.
pitfalls: Fallible acquisition must stay in main's call tree: an exception escaping a namespace-scope initialiser is not catchable from main and calls std::terminate.
Warm-up that runs before logging and configuration are wired produces failures nobody can see - order the boot sequence explicitly.
std::async's default policy may defer the callable, so 'eager' requires launch::async if the work must actually start now.

variants.name: pre-main static initialisation (classic)
variants.idiom_name: objects with static storage duration + construct-on-first-use
variants.implementation_notes: The classic realisation: namespace-scope objects acquire during the pre-main phase, so no caller can reach them uninitialised and the pattern needs no explicit call site. The price is the static initialisation order fiasco - order across translation units is unspecified, and GCC documents that the order between C++ static-storage objects and constructor-attribute functions is normally unspecified as well - so anything that depends on another object must use construct-on-first-use (a function-local static) or the non-portable init_priority attribute.
pitfalls: Static initialisation order across translation units is unspecified, so an initialiser that touches another namespace-scope object races the linker.
An exception escaping a pre-main initialiser terminates the program before main with no handler and usually a poor diagnostic.
Destruction order is the reverse of construction only within one translation unit, so matching release needs the same ordering discipline.

variants.name: pre-allocated memory arenas (std::pmr)
variants.idiom_name: std::pmr::synchronized_pool_resource / monotonic buffers built at start-up
variants.implementation_notes: Here the eagerly acquired resource is the allocator itself: build a std::pmr::synchronized_pool_resource (or a monotonic buffer for a request-scoped arena) during start-up and give it to the hot-path containers, so per-request allocation never reaches the global allocator and cannot introduce an unpredictable lock or page-fault cost inside the deadline. Use it when the hot path is allocation-heavy and the memory profile is known; it complements, and does not replace, connection or model warm-up.
pitfalls: Memory held by a pool resource is not returned to the OS until the resource dies, so an over-sized pre-warm looks exactly like a leak.
A monotonic buffer must be reset per scope (never shared across requests) or it grows without bound.
Mixing containers from different memory resources in one hot path destroys the locality the variant was chosen for.
